topStories.headline: Bruma, a Fog-Inspired Cocktail Lounge, Opens Monday at the Ritz-Carlton on Nob Hill
topStories.dek: The Ritz-Carlton's new lobby bar draws on San Francisco's coastal mist and the neighborhood's Gilded Age glamour when it opens October 12.
topStories.body:
Nob Hill's hotel row adds another destination this week: Bruma, a new cocktail lounge and all-day salon inside the Ritz-Carlton's landmark 1909 Neoclassical building at 600 Stockton Street, opens Monday, October 12. The 80-seat space was designed by the firm Fettle using a palette of aged brass, ocean navy, and espresso brown, with a custom mural that nods to the surrounding neighborhood.

Named for the Spanish word for "mist," the concept takes its cues from San Francisco's iconic coastal fog. The beverage program is organized into four thematic passages — World's Edge, Open Water, Golden City, and High Ground — and features signature ceremonies including a tableside martini chilled with liquid nitrogen and a reimagined Nob Hill Pisco Punch finished with pineapple brûlée. Food comes from Executive Chef George Vanyi, who developed a menu of Modern California lounge fare in collaboration with Lowder-Tascarella Hospitality.

Bruma is intended to function as a gathering place through the full arc of a day: afternoon tea, golden-hour aperitivo, evening cocktails, and late-night conversation. The lounge's regular weekly programming includes aperitivo on Wednesdays and Thursdays from 4 to 6 p.m., live jazz on Fridays from 7 to 10 p.m., and a Latin fusion band on Saturdays.

The opening adds to a run of hospitality investment on the hill. The Huntington Hotel reopened in March after a six-year closure, and the Big Four restaurant returned the same month in its 50th anniversary year. Bruma does not replace Parallel 37, the Ritz-Carlton's existing restaurant, but occupies the hotel lobby as a separate concept.

topStories.headline: Eviction Scare for 92-Year-Old Nob Hill Tenant Pushes SF Supervisors Toward New Law
topStories.dek: Sue Yeng Yan has lived in her rent-controlled Jackson Street apartment since 1982; after a landlord used a clutter complaint to threaten her removal, two supervisors are now drafting legislation to protect tenants citywide.
topStories.body:
Sue Yeng Yan, 92, has lived in her rent-controlled apartment at 1120 Jackson Street — along the Powell-Hyde cable car line in Lower Nob Hill — since 1982, paying $281.42 a month. In March, she received an eviction notice claiming her apartment was a nuisance because of clutter. Four other tenants in the 16-unit building received identically worded notices at the same time; at least three were senior citizens.

The notices came from Nabob Hill LLC, an Los Angeles-based company that purchased the building in July 2025 for $1.5 million. The listing had described the units' rents as "significantly below market" and touted an estimated 224 percent rental upside achievable through tenant turnover. The landlord's attorneys said the notices were meant only to bring units into compliance, but tenants and advocates said the effort amounted to a pretext for displacing long-term residents.

Yan's son-in-law and eviction defense attorney Kit Wong told the SF Standard that Yan has not recovered from the ordeal. Under current rules, Nabob Hill LLC could restart eviction proceedings at any time; the notice it served stated that "future inspections may occur."

The case drew enough attention that Supervisors Myrna Melgar and Jackie Fielder have prepared legislation to change how nuisance evictions work in San Francisco. According to the SF Standard, which first reported on the proposed law on October 5, the bill would give tenants a chance to remedy alleged conditions before losing their homes. Hoodline reported on October 7 that nuisance evictions citywide are up 41 percent, lending urgency to the proposal. A hearing date had not yet been announced as of press time.

topStories.headline: Chinatown's $150 Million Construction Push Rolls On — and the Broadway Tunnel Is Still Running at Half Capacity
topStories.dek: Two months into a 14-month partial closure, drivers and Muni riders should expect continued delays through the Broadway Tunnel as crews work on all three simultaneous Chinatown projects.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's Chinatown entered the latest phase of its $150 million infrastructure overhaul this summer, and the disruptions are ongoing. Three major projects — the $73 million Portsmouth Square renovation, the seismic upgrade of the Chinatown Public Health Center, and the renovation of the Chinatown/Him Mark Lai Branch Library — are being managed simultaneously by SF Public Works, with construction expected to continue into 2028.

The Broadway Tunnel, which runs beneath Russian Hill and connects the neighborhood to Chinatown, has been operating at reduced capacity since August 17. One bore at a time is being closed for approximately seven months each, keeping a single lane open in each direction throughout the 14-month project. The eastbound bore into Chinatown was closed first; motorists should expect peak-hour delays through October 2027. SF Public Works announced the partial closure schedule in a July 20 press release. SFMTA traffic controllers are stationed near the tunnel entrance to assist navigation.

At Portsmouth Square, demolition of the elevated pedestrian bridge connecting the park to the Hilton Chinatown is complete, and construction fencing now surrounds the 1.3-acre plaza, which will remain closed until approximately mid-2028. The renovation will add an 8,300-square-foot community clubhouse with meeting rooms and a commercial kitchen, a larger playground, an adult fitness area, and a performance plaza. The project is funded primarily through the 2020 Health and Recovery Bond and developer impact fees.

The Chinatown/Him Mark Lai Branch Library is also closed for a 30-month renovation. During construction, Chinatown Public Health Center services have been relocated to the nearby Chinese Hospital. Drivers navigating the area can find detour maps and live updates on transit impacts at SFMTA.com/ChinatownParking.

events.title: Chinatown Night Market — Final 2026 Date
events.description: The season finale of the monthly Chinatown Night Market, voted the #1 night market in the country for the second consecutive year, takes over five blocks of Grant Avenue with food vendors, lion dancing, cultural performances, outdoor dining, and a beer and wine garden. Free admission; no tickets required.

events.title: Russian Hill Neighbors Monthly Cleanup
events.location: NW corner of Filbert St. & Hyde St., Russian Hill
events.description: Russian Hill Neighbors, Refuse Refuse, SF Public Works, and the Civic Joy Fund host their monthly neighborhood cleanup. Volunteers meet at 9:30 a.m. for coffee and donuts before fanning out at 10 a.m.; all supplies provided. Free; register at mobilize.us/civicjoyfund/event/757464.

events.title: Kloetzel Chapman Duo: The Women of Note Project
events.location: Old First Presbyterian Church, 1751 Sacramento St., Polk Gulch
events.description: Cellist Jennifer Kloetzel and pianist Allegra Chapman perform their ongoing multi-season project celebrating cello and piano repertoire written by women, with works by Hélène Liebmann, Luise Le Beau, Mel Bonis, and Leokadiya Kashperova. Tickets: $30 general, $25 seniors, $10 students; a livestream option is also available.

events.title: Unplugged: A Typewriter Poetry Event
events.location: Russian Hill Bookstore, 2162 Polk St., Russian Hill
events.description: The independent bookstore on upper Polk Street hosts a guided typewriter poetry session — participants explore the art of the form through writing prompts and creative community. Check Eventbrite for ticket availability; space is limited.

events.title: Yale Whiffenpoofs at Grace Cathedral
events.location: Grace Cathedral, 1100 California St., Nob Hill
events.description: The Whiffenpoofs of 2026 — Yale's renowned a cappella ensemble, founded in 1909 — perform a diverse repertoire spanning vocal jazz, folk, pop, and Broadway inside the cathedral's Gothic Revival nave. Tickets $17; details at gracecathedral.org.

events.title: Grace Cathedral Sound Bath
events.location: Grace Cathedral, 1100 California St., Nob Hill
events.description: A meditative Sound Bath experience inside the soaring architecture of Grace Cathedral, where light filters through stained glass windows during the 90-minute session. Tickets and registration at gracecathedral.org.

events.title: Halloween Storytime in Francisco Park
events.description: Francisco Park Conservancy hosts a Halloween-themed Storytime on the park's Main Lawn, recommended for children ages 3–5. Bring a blanket and a snack; suggested donation $10, with a free option for park stewards.

events.title: FITNESS SF Polk Grand Opening
events.location: FITNESS SF Polk, 1600 Jackson St. (at Polk), Polk Gulch
events.description: The locally owned FITNESS SF chain opens its ninth Bay Area location in the former Lombardi Sports building, bringing a 42,000-square-foot gym with strength and cardio areas, group fitness classes, red-light therapy, a dry sauna, and free parking to the Polk corridor. Founding memberships are still available at fitnesssf.com.

moreNews.headline: Bruma's Opening Is the Latest Chapter in Nob Hill's Hotel Renaissance
moreNews.body: With Bruma debuting at the Ritz-Carlton on October 12 and the Huntington Hotel having reopened in March after a six-year pandemic closure, Nob Hill is in the midst of a sustained hospitality revival. The Huntington's reopening restored two beloved anchors: the Big Four restaurant — which returned on March 17 in its 50th anniversary year — and the three-level Nob Hill Spa. Designer Ken Fulk led the Huntington's interior renovation, which preserved the building's 1920s Italian Renaissance Revival architecture while adding 143 updated rooms and suites. Mayor Daniel Lurie attended a ribbon-cutting and sign-relighting ceremony at the Huntington in early March.

moreNews.headline: Dads with Strollers Returns to Francisco Park This Sunday
moreNews.body: The recurring Dads with Strollers meetup at Francisco Park in Russian Hill is scheduled for Sunday, October 11, from 10 a.m. to noon on the park's lawn. The free, drop-in gathering is open to parents and caregivers of all kinds. Francisco Park, the 4.5-acre park on the site of a former reservoir at the crest of Russian Hill, is operated by SF Recreation & Parks.
